bibliography.abstract: Abstract Eco-villages have emerged as laboratories of alternative socio-spatial organisation, generating practices that may inform the retrofitting of mainstream low-density housing settlements. This paper examines how principles developed in Danish eco-villages can be translated into settlements that share comparable spatial typologies, such as suburban areas, peri-urban districts, and small towns characterised by dispersed morphology and limited shared infrastructure, but differ in their underlying socio-spatial conditions. Based on fieldwork in three communities—Andelssamfundet i Hjortshøj, Karise Permatopia, and Svanholm—the study draws on semi-structured interviews, spatial observations, and GIS-based geo-surveys. Using an analytical framework focused on community, built environment, and ecology, it identifies strategies linking collective agency with everyday resource stewardship. While the three cases share sustainability-oriented values, they differ in governance and socio-ecological organisation: Hjortshøj emphasises informal collaboration, Permatopia integrates family-oriented permaculture routines, and Svanholm represents structured collectivism and agricultural production. The paper argues that retrofitting requires translation rather than replication. Because social organisation and spatial form are mutually constitutive, selective adaptation must extend beyond spatial typologies to the governance routines and participation infrastructures that sustain collective life. Such translation is enabled by sustained institutional support and shared spatial resources, but is constrained by self-selection dynamics, unequal access, and volunteer dependency.

en.caveats: The findings are based on self-selected, highly motivated eco-communities, which may limit their direct translation to mainstream suburban populations that lack similar volunteer capacity or shared values.
en.what: This study analyzes how socio-spatial practices from three Danish eco-villages (Andelssamfundet i Hjortshøj, Karise Permatopia, and Svanholm) can inform retrofitting strategies for low-density suburban and peri-urban settlements. Using semi-structured interviews, spatial observations, and GIS-based geo-surveys, the research examines how different governance models—ranging from informal collaboration to structured collectivism—link collective agency with resource stewardship.
en.why: It demonstrates that retrofitting low-density suburbs requires translating governance routines and participation infrastructures rather than merely replicating physical spatial typologies, showing how social organization and spatial form must be adapted together.
